confidence_note: Verified in a full text of the book (commitment chapter, ch. 2, decision chapter). Old text's 'maybe a better one exists' examples are dropped; 'commitment feels like a loss of freedom then gains identity' is replaced by Brooks's own freedom-to versus freedom-from passage. Commitment is Brooks's argument, not a finding.
facts: Brooks writes that after several years of pursuing open options 'it's not so much that you lose the thread of the meaning of your life; you have trouble even staying focused on the question.'

He notes people deliberate more over small choices than big ones: before buying a car they read ratings and check resale values; for a vocation they 'just sort of slide rather than decide'; they marry the person they happen to be living with.
'On the first mountain, a person makes individual choices and keeps their options open. The second mountain is a vale of promise making.'

Most of us make four big commitments: to a vocation, to a spouse and family, to a philosophy or faith, to a community. All require a vow, an investment of time and effort, 'a willingness to close off other options'.

A commitment is 'making a promise to something without expecting a return'; 'I can't not do this.' A contract is weighing pros and cons and the person does not change; a commitment 'changes who you are'.

A commitment is love and promise 'put under law': people bind their future selves to obligations for moments when feelings falter ('falling in love with something and then building a structure of behavior around it for those moments when love falters').
'Our commitments give us our identity. They are how we introduce ourselves to strangers.'

'Freedom from' versus 'freedom to': 'You have to chain yourself to the piano and practice for year after year if you want to have the freedom to really play.' Tim Keller: real freedom 'is not so much the absence of restrictions as finding the right ones.'
'A thick life is defined by commitments and obligations. The life well lived is a journey from open options to sweet compulsions.'
Brooks quotes L. A. Paul on the big choices of life: 'You shouldn't fool yourself, you have no idea what you are getting into.'
Brooks: deep commitment 'happens when some person or cause or field of research has become part of your very identity': 'I'm a musician. I'm a scientist. I'm a Marine.'
Brooks notes that 'commitment' derives from the Latin mittere, 'to send': the committed person sends herself out and gives another a claim.
scene_details: a car bought after reading the ratings and the resale values
a career slid into because someone gave you a job
a person chained to the piano year after year
tension: People research a car for days and slide into a career and a marriage; Brooks says the second kind of choice is where freedom is actually spent.
opening_idea: Open on the car bought after reading every rating next to the career entered by sliding.

lessons.idea: Choose what to give up on purpose, and bind your future self to it; the structure keeps you going when the feeling fades.
lessons.anchor: The piano chain and the commitments built under law.
lessons.example: A runner who signs up for a spring race and books a Saturday group run so the plan survives a tired week.

reflect_final: Which one commitment in your life do you actually keep because of a structure around it, and what would a similar structure do for the one you keep postponing?

use_cases.situation: You keep postponing a decision about a path you half-want.
use_cases.move: Write down what you would have to close off to commit, as Brooks says every commitment requires, and see whether you still want it.

use_cases.situation: A friend has drifted between options for years.
use_cases.move: Ask what they would be willing to chain themselves to, like the pianist; avoid telling them what to choose.

use_cases.situation: A partner and you both avoid naming your commitment.
use_cases.move: Ask what structure around it would keep you going on a tired week.

pocket_idea: Brooks says you chain yourself to the piano to gain the freedom to play: pick the chain, not just the wish.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: People study the ratings before buying a car and slide into a career, Brooks says, though the big choices need the most deliberation.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Brooks sees people deliberate over cars and drift into jobs and marriages; his answer is commitment, a promise with a structure around it, with freedom as the freedom to play, bought by years at the piano.
